newsitem.title: PERU: Conditions worse than ever for hostages in Lima.
newsitem.headline: Conditions worse than ever for hostages in Lima.

text.p: Now without electricity for the first time, conditions for around 340 hostages held by leftist guerrillas in Peru worsened on Sunday as the government ignored requests to restore vital services.

Police even stopped Red Cross workers from ferrying in lanterns during the night to illuminate the gloom inside the residence, whose elegant portals belie the squalor that released hostages say lies within.
Fuel for the power generator used by the rebels ran out on Saturday and there was no response from the authorities to repeated pleas for fresh supplies.
Running water, mains electricity and cellular phone links with the building have been cut off for days, apparently as part of the government's tough strategy to wear down the rebels.
Released captives have told horror stories of stinking overcrowded toilets, smart clothes turned to filthy togs after being worn for five days on humid, overpowering heat.

Local news reports say the 340 hostages are crammed into an eight-room residence, sleeping packed on the floors of a building normally inhabited by just six people. A top Peruvian doctor has warned of the risk of a cholera epidemic.

News media camped outside the besieged residence have caught sight of hostages appearing occasionally at the barred and fortified windows of the building but none has shown so far any obvious sign of distress.

The hostages have complained in messages sent out of the residence and in handwritten posters held up to a window that the lack of services is hurting them more than their captors but the government has not been moved.
On the brighter side, all the hostages say their captors have treated them well. There have been no reports of physical violence against the captives or verbal abuse.
"I believe their slogan was to give respectful treatment," released hostage Javier Sota told a local newspaper.
"At no time did they use swear words. Of course we were hostages and we had to obey but the distribution of food was our sole responsibility."

The VIP captives, who were enjoying a lavish sushi buffet when Marxist rebels stormed the residence last Tuesday, have had to make do with sandwiches and cake since. A newspaper said their daily rations were worth just $1.50 per person.
Adding to their frustration, captives at the barred residence windows could watch birds descending from the sky to snap up the remains of Tuesday's buffet from the marquee on the lawn outside.

Captive Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki said in a walkie-talkie conversation on Saturday that some of his colleagues were "seriously ill" but mediators described the captives' ailments so far as relatively minor, with diarrhoea prevailing.

Released hostages say they have whiled away the long hours inside the residence playing parlour games brought in by the Red Cross, reading magazines and books and debating politics with their captors.

Photographs smuggled out of the residence and shown on television on Saturday depicted some of the hostages sitting around inside looking apparently well but it was not clear when the images had been shot or whether they reflected the conditions all the captives were living under.
